title: Explicit values in Zig
summary: Declare typed values, iterate a slice with a capture, and count positives.

scenario.briefing: A rover telemetry check counts positive wheel-speed deltas in Zig.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Predict the result of the same counting rule on new input.

hints: The for loop already visits every value.
Compare the captured value with zero.
Use an if statement around the increment.
Add if (value > 0) { count += 1; } inside the loop.

misconceptions.description: Counting zero as a positive delta.
misconceptions.testDescription: The for loop binds each value and counts only positives.
misconceptions.feedback: The test is value > 0. Zero and negative values must not increment the count.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a const binding can be reassigned.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Declaring count with const, then using count += 1 in the loop.
misconceptions.feedback: const prevents reassignment. Use var for a value that changes, and keep the type explicit.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a Zig variable can change type after assignment.
misconceptions.feedback: Zig is statically typed. A variable keeps its declared type; only its value changes.

misconceptions.description: Counting every element instead of the positive ones.
misconceptions.feedback: The function increments only when value > 0. An array length includes zero and negative values.

sections.title: Every value has a type
sections.body: Zig checks types at compile time. A function signature states each parameter and return type, so countPositive takes a slice of i32 values and returns u32. A const binding cannot be reassigned, while a var binding can change and needs an explicit type.

sections.title: Slices carry a length
sections.body: A slice is a pointer plus a length, written []const i32 for read-only integers. Indexing stays inside that length, and safe builds panic on an out-of-bounds access instead of reading unrelated memory.

sections.title: For loops capture elements
sections.body: The form for (values) |value| binds each element in order without an index variable. When the index matters, for (values, 0..) |value, index| provides both values.

vocabulary.definition: A pointer and a length that view a contiguous sequence.
A name that cannot be reassigned after initialization.
The |value| clause that binds each element during a for loop.

localVerification.description: Compiles and runs the program with the Zig compiler, printing the counted total.

tests.description: The function keeps the typed slice parameter and return type.
The for loop binds each value and counts only positives.

steps.title: Types and slices
hints: A slice carries a pointer and a length.
Zig does not allow a variable to change type.

statements.label: A function parameter in Zig declares its type in the signature.
A const binding cannot be reassigned after it is initialized.
A slice stores a pointer and a length.
A Zig variable can hold a value of a different type after assignment.

steps.explanation: Zig is statically typed: the compiler knows every parameter and return type. const prevents reassignment, var allows it, and a slice combines a pointer with a length used for bounds checks.

steps.title: Run the same rule
steps.prompt: countPositive receives the slice { 4, 0, -3, 7 }. What does it return?
hints: The function counts values strictly greater than zero.
The negative value is not counted either.

quiz.prompt: countPositive receives the slice { 4, 0, -3, 7 }. What does it return?

options.label: 4, because the slice length is returned
0, because the count starts at zero

quiz.explanation: Only 4 and 7 satisfy value > 0, so the counter reaches two.
